headline: Price, perception and the 5% you spend foolishly
intro: First round. Hormozi, Alchemy and Unreasonable Hospitality do most of the talking, with a bit of future-you, then Thai for the street stall.

items.label: Recall
items.prompt: Hormozi pushed an underpriced health company to raise its price by 50%. What happened to their close rate?
options: It dropped, but profit per sale made up for it
It went up, because the old price made people doubt it worked
It stayed flat, so the extra margin was pure profit
It went up, because the sales team was paid more commission
items.explain: Price is a signal. When the price says 'budget option', the right buyers tune out before you pitch. The only thing worse than selling a $1,000 thing to a $100 buyer is selling a $100 thing to a $1,000 buyer.

items.label: Who said it

ideas.title: You live with the story of a decision
ideas.note: What would you tomorrow want you today to do?

items.prompt: Match each line to the person it came from.
pairs: Luxury means just giving more; hospitality means being more thoughtful.
You live with the story of your decisions far longer than their impact.
Big improvements in perception cost a fraction of the same improvement in reality.
items.explain: Five sources, one thread: how something feels and where it's heading matters more than the raw facts of it.

items.label: Recall

ideas.title: Not buying? Qualify or educate
ideas.note: What to do when leads aren't buying

items.prompt: Leads are turning up but not buying. Hormozi says it's one of two problems. What are they, and what's the fix for each?
items.answer: Either they don't meet the criteria to buy (fix: tighter qualification, and tell the lead source 'more like these good ones'), or they don't want it enough yet (fix: more education, like a VSL before the call, a video while they wait, proof to consume).
items.explain: His line: if they're there, educate, which is to say sell. The Boulder park VSL ended up being the best thing on the page and the best ad.

items.text: Trust grows at the speed of a coconut tree and falls at the speed of a coconut.
items.mark: falls at the speed of a coconut

items.label: Apply it · two books, one move
items.scenario: Rory Sutherland: making a train 20% faster costs hundreds of millions, making it 20% more enjoyable costs almost nothing. Will Guidara: manage 95% of the business to the penny, spend the last 5% 'foolishly'.
items.prompt: Pick one client. What's the 5% you'd spend foolishly to make their customer's experience 20% better? Be specific about the moment it lands.
items.answer: Cheap, personal, visible gestures at a moment that matters beat bigger spend. Guidara's $2 hot dog beat caviar because only that table could have got it. Endings count double: a gracious gesture at the end can outweigh everything before it.
items.yourNote: What are some low cost ways I could make the experience of my clients' products 20% more enjoyable? Sending a joke along with the packaging. Or even a personalised thank you.

items.label: Put it in order
items.prompt: The theme park was weeks from going under. Put Hormozi's cash rescue in the order he ran it.
items: Launch a 7 to 10 day giveaway (win the whole summer free)
Hammer the list with email and ads while the countdown runs
Phone every lead that came in
Move the non-winners onto the standard summer offer
Run the same play again for a new occasion (birthday parties)
items.explain: Cash was the constraint, so: leads, then sell the leads, then let the cash fund capacity. 3,700 leads and a 325% jump in camp sales. Then the bottleneck moved to sales staff, not lead flow.

items.label: Fill the gap

ideas.title: Trust goes next to the button

items.prompt: On the park's landing page, the parent ratings were moved. The rule: trust belongs next to the ___, not somewhere else on the page.
items.explain: Put the proof right where the doubt happens, at the button. Same page: four banners cut to one, and a specific stat ('zero falls last year') instead of a vague safety claim.

items.label: Recall
items.prompt: Seth Godin says word spreads because customers talk about you. What makes them actually do it?
options: You post often enough that you stay front of mind
You give them something to say that helps them or raises their status
You ask every happy customer for a review
You're more authentic than the competition
items.explain: Marketing is creating the conditions for other people to spread your idea. Also from that episode: AI should make your thing better, not just cheaper. You can't cost-reduce yourself to greatness.

items.label: Apply it · your life

ideas.title: What would tomorrow-you want?
ideas.note: What would you tomorrow want you today to do?

items.scenario: JL Collins: if your lifestyle rises with your income, you're not free. Chris Williamson: ask 'what would tomorrow-you want today-you to do?'
items.prompt: What savings rate does JL Collins aim for? Then name one money or time decision coming up this week where both ideas point the same way, and what you'll do.
items.answer: 50%, and the keenest go for 70 to 80%. Lifestyle creep is the real golden handcuffs; every dollar not spent buys future-you freedom. Williamson's test pulls you out of the moment so you decide for yourself in 24 hours, 24 days and 24 months.

items.text: Inspiration is perishable. Act on it immediately.

items.label: Recall
items.prompt: Night Nurse's scientists nearly scrapped their cold and flu formula. What saved it?
options: They cut the dose until the side effects went away
Marketing turned the drowsiness into the selling point: a night-time remedy
They sold it at a premium so people trusted it more
They put it in a smaller bottle so it felt stronger
items.explain: A masterclass in reframing: the flaw became the feature. The two wrong answers that sound plausible are also Alchemy ideas (reassuringly expensive aspirin, Red Bull's small can).

items.label: Thai · from your notes
items.prompt: Match the Thai to the English.
pairs: I don't want it / no thanks
items.explain: Your note says nam khaeng is 'water with ice'. Strictly it's ice itself, so 'khor nam khaeng' gets you a glass of ice. Plain drinking water is 'nam plao'. And mai ow takes a falling tone, not the rising 'mai' of a question.

items.label: Thai · from the course
items.prompt: Could you please speak slowly? Chuay puut ___ noy krab.
items.thai: ช่วยพูดช้าๆ หน่อยครับ
items.explain: Chuay (said 'shoy') is 'could you', chaa chaa is 'slowly'. Its twin: chuay puut eek krang noy krab, 'could you say that again?'

items.label: Thai · from the course
items.prompt: You point at something on the stall and say "Nee tao rai krab?" What have you asked?
items.thai: นี่เท่าไหร่ครับ
items.explain: Tao rai is 'how much'. The others, from your Lesson 4 and 5 notes: Nee a-rai (what is this), Nee khorng khrai (whose is this), yuu teenai (where is it). Swap nee for nan to ask about 'that'.

items.label: Thai · say it

ideas.title: Pom phuut paa-saa Thai nit noi

items.prompt: How do you say "I speak a little Thai"? Type it how it sounds.
items.answer: Pom phuut paa-saa Thai (dai) nit noi krab
items.speak: ผมพูดภาษาไทยได้นิดหน่อยครับ
items.explain: Your teacher Sassi's tip: say it slowly. If you rush, people assume you're a foreigner speaking English and don't hear the Thai. Adding 'dai' (can) is optional and a touch more natural.

thaiTask.title: Order a whole meal at a street stall in Thai, start to finish

phrase.thai: โชคดีนะครับ
phrase.meaning: Literally 'good luck', used like 'have a good one' when you leave.

thaiTask.where: Any khao man gai or noodle stall, or the smoothie cart near your place. Somewhere you'll go back to, so they start to recognise you.
steps: Order with a plate count: "Khor khao man gai neung jan krab" (one plate of chicken rice).
If they come back at you fast: "Pom phuut paa-saa Thai nit noi. Chuay puut chaa chaa noy krab."
Pay with "Tao rai krab?" and leave with "Khop khun krab, chok dee na krab."
Do it at three different stalls before the next task lands.
thaiTask.stretch: Ask the owner "Bpen yang rai baang krab?" (how's it going?) and see how far you get.
